To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) 5α‐Reductase Deficiency Syndrome (5α‐RD), a disorder of sex development ( DSD ), results in a male phenotype with female‐like external genitalia and a 46,XX karyotype.

(1) the sex chromosome complement and gonadal hormones are important factors that shape brain and behavior, but the extent to which they do so is dependent on the type of DSD and the individual's sex chromosome complement; (2) the presence of Y chromosomes in males with CAIS or 5α‐RedD is associated with a more masculinized brain and behavior, whereas the presence of a Y chromosome in males with CAH is associated with a less masculinized brain; and
sex differences in the brain and in behavior are determined largely, but not entirely, by genetic sex and by in utero gonadally derived hormones.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how sex differences in the brain are shaped by genetic and hormonal factors during prenatal and postnatal development.
the effects of gonadal hormones on the development of the human brain and behavior.
how genetic, hormonal, and social factors shape brain and behavioral sex differences.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the sex of the brain is determined by a combination of genetic sex, in utero hormonal exposure, and postnatal hormonal milieu.
genetic and environmental influences interact with one another to shape brain development and post‐natal behavior.
the effects of gonadal hormones on the brain are highly dependent on the sex chromosome composition and that sex differences in the brain are not solely dependent on gonadal hormones.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the sex of the brain is not necessarily the same as the sex of the body.
the brain and behavior are shaped by both chromosomal sex and gonadal hormone exposure.
the sex chromosome and gonadal hormones are the primary determinants of brain and behavioral phenotypic differences between males and females.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of genetic sex and gonadal hormones on brain and behavior are complex and cannot be easily separated.

genetic sex and gonadal hormone exposure are the primary determinants of sex‐specific phenotypes in the human brain and behavior, but that social influences are likely to have an impact on these processes.
the sex differences in brain development are not simply due to genetic sex or hormonal exposure.
